paragraphs.text: Dear elders and sisters, I hope today has been one of your best so far. I know we had some baptisms and I know there are more souls that are preparing for the Covenant under your inspired guidance and teaching. I got some great reports today from the assistants in our meeting about their follow-up calls and I just want you to know I am so proud of you and I'm grateful to serve with you. Now before you get too comfortable with my compliments, even though my words are sincere, I know that each of you have your moments of weakness and times when you make a wrong choice. We all do. That is part of the process of mortal probation.

The question is always, what do you do after that bad decision or after that foolish action? That's the question. What do you do? Do you learn? Do you get better, stronger, and especially smarter? Or do you go right on like the man who has to repeat the same mistake over and over again because he's too undisciplined to learn from his own mistakes? Or he's too prideful to even admit he made a mistake? That's the question.

Self-control, self-discipline—these are two ways of saying the same thing. Have you gained enough control or discipline over your natural man to be able to use your agency wisely enough that your agency actually expands? Or are you so undisciplined that you use your agency so poorly that it gradually gets smaller and smaller and smaller? You see, that's what happens. When a person uses their agency wisely, they get more and more freedom. When a person uses their agency badly, they get less and less freedom. The people who use their agency the worst, they end up in prison. Their agency is completely gone, basically, in terms of any kind of freedom. The people who use their agency super wisely, they grow in their influence and capacity that the whole world becomes their available place to do their thing and enjoy their life and add value in their way.

Now, speaking of the world, in many ways, our global economy today is based on addiction. If businesses can push your buttons in a way that can get you addicted to their product or their service, then they can own you. So businesses literally focus on trying to figure out what your most basic urges are. They try to figure out what kind of food you really crave. They try to figure out what kind of activities you just can't pull yourself away from. And as they learn what drives you, then they keep supplying you with that until you literally are no more than a slave. You think you're free, but you can't put down that food. Every time you see it, you've got to have it. You can't put down that game on the smartphone. You can't put down that particular activity. You just can't do it. You say you can, but you keep going back to it because you're addicted. And these businesses, they actually create those addictions in you on purpose. I've talked to you about this kind of stuff before, but it's really true. And so I still see some of you making those mistakes and it saddens me because if you don't learn it in the mission field, you're probably not going to learn it afterwards.

Now deeply inside, none of you, nobody really wants to be unhealthy and practice self-destructive habits. But if you look around yourself, you see people everywhere doing things that basically shorten their lives every single day. Now death doesn't come immediately, maybe, but it's going to arrive way earlier than it should because of the way they're taking care of themselves—or I should say, not taking care of themselves. Diabetes, cancer, heart disease—these diseases are lifestyle diseases. They account for 80% of all the early deaths in the world. Staggering, isn't it? And every one of those deaths come as a function of the choices people made on just basically two types of choices.

Profit to businesses really doesn't care about your health. It doesn't care about anything but profit to the company. Now I'm a businessman, I want profit, but you need to understand how to own yourself in such a way that you can sift through the different things that are going on around you and make choices that are good for you, not just do what businesses want you to do.

So let's take a look at this and let's look at just one thing. Let's imagine a life in which you learned how to control yourself so that the obstacles the world throws at you, the tricks they throw at you, the buttons they try to push on you become irrelevant. You just have enough mental toughness, enough self-control, enough self-discipline that you just kind of power on, proceeding with your goals day by day. Instead of putting junk food into your body, you eat healthy foods. You don't eat too much, you don't eat too often. You allow yourself a little reward every now and then, but not too much. This will make a tremendous impact on your health, far more than you think. You no longer have to try out fancy fad diets. If you eat real food instead of fast food or processed food and you control the amounts you eat, you won't become overweight no matter how much you want that other junk stuff.

If you also begin leading an active lifestyle, you get up, you move around. I know we're in the apartments a lot, but you can get up, you can do push-ups, you can do sit-ups, you can run in place, you can do a lot of things. If you exercise three times a week for about 150 minutes, if you walk a few miles, literally after just one year of controlling those two areas, your diet and your exercise, you would literally transform your life—not just your body, but your life.

Your health is a big area that you can improve if you have more self-control or more self-discipline, but there's another area that's even more important. Think about your time. Your time. The most precious asset you have in your life is your time. If you waste your time each day, you can never get it back. You can mess up your health and most of the time you can get it back, but you can't get back your time. In the world we live in now, we're bombarded with entertainment: television, video games, the internet. All these things have their uses, but without self-control, they can become super harmful to you. Most people don't have enough self-control, and as a result, they end up spending way too much time on video games, or watching TV, or mindlessly browsing the internet. They end up ruining their lives in some cases.

I had to fire one of my top executives, a guy that was in a bishopric, a guy that was in his 40s. He had a wife and five children. He was a guy with a very high-end education, had a Master's of Business Administration. I mean, he was an executive drawing a big six-figure income in dollars every year; had to fire him because he was addicted to playing a video game during the workday. I mean, how crazy is that? But it happens. It happens a lot, because once you get addicted, well, remember what I told you? You're a slave.

How about instead of wasting all of your time watching other people do stuff, playing video games, browsing the internet, mindlessly just wandering around in cyberspace, or even worse, wasting your time on things that are totally inappropriate? How about instead of doing that, what you do instead is you commit to reading two hours a day? Now, you should be doing that right now. In the mission field, you got this great opportunity to read the scriptures and other great writings of the prophets. Read that two hours a day. It sounds like a lot, but it shouldn't be to you, but ask yourself how many hours you waste even in the mission field on stuff that is just wasting your life.

Books are life-changing. Books have changed my life. We can learn through experience, but you can only have so much time. You can't get as much experience as you need to have to be super effective unless you learn from other people. And all these people have written books that you can actually learn from their experience by reading and studying the book. With books, you can actually dramatically double, triple, quadruple, or even more your learning without having to actually spend the time doing it because you can learn it through a book.

Now, a year goes by. You've been reading two hours a day for 12 months. I'm not going to try to estimate the number of books you'd read—it depends on how fast you read—but there's one thing you can be sure of: the number of books you would read by reading two hours a day in one year would be more than most people will read in their lifetimes. In the average person's whole life, according to statistics, they won't read even half the books you could read as an average reader in one year by reading just two hours a day.

But reading great books without applying what you learn won't lead you to completely changing your life. You need to take action on what you learn. For every single problem you experience in your life, there's at least one decent book that offers the solution. To most of your issues, there's dozens of great books. So now as you start utilizing your knowledge, taking it, putting it into action, because of your self-control, you take these actions instead of procrastinating. You're smarter in your actions. You grow in that cycle of learning that we've talked about in the five steps so often. Imagine how many obstacles you could overcome and how fast you could move up in society and the economy.

But let's take it further. Sometimes as you're reading for two hours a day on a daily basis, you eventually become inspired to write down a few of your own thoughts on paper. You realize that you'd love to write a book. The fact is, more than 80% of the people in the world would like to write a book, but only 1% of them will ever write a book. And you know why the 99% fail? Yeah, you guessed it—lack of self-control to do the right thing, the thing they want to do, instead of letting their moods and their appetites decide the flow of their day and how they spend their time. Fortunately, that's no longer a problem for you. So you commit to writing just 500 words a day. And you stick to that for another 12 months. At the end of that year, you end up with more than 180,000 words of content. Now the average book written today is only 90,000 words, so you have, in just one year, written twice the average book. Now, it may not be War and Peace or some great piece of literature—it might be, but it's probably not going to be—but hey, it's a miracle anyway compared to what you used to do before you learned the skill and gained the muscle of self-control.

Let's assume the positive, however, because why not? Why not assume the positive? Let's say your book turns out to be pretty decent. A few people that you share it with give you some very positive feedback. So you hire an editor and a graphic designer to prepare it for publishing. And because of the self-publishing movement that's going on right now, you no longer even need to get a publishing house or an agent. You can just publish it yourself on Amazon and let the readers judge your words. More and more positive reviews come in. The money starts rolling in. Over time you become a recognized author and you like it so much that you continue getting better at it and maybe you even quit your job. Every year now you add another book or two to your portfolio.

Taking this story even further in your imagination will cause you to be so inspired that you can realize that not only writing, but you can build other skills. You can create other invaluable skills to your portfolio of skills literally by taking control of your day and dedicating an hour or two for a year on building that skill until you become a master in it. Some people would say that this sounds nice when you read it or hear it, but doing it is a whole lot different, and that's true. It's absolutely hard to do big things, to do hard things. But let's be honest, elders and sisters, why would you expect a miracle, a complete life transformation by just doing little easy stupid things? Nobody's going to transform their life in a positive way by playing video games. Nobody's going to transform their life in a positive way by just mindlessly surfing the web.

You've heard the old saying that there are three types of people in the world. Type number one: those who make things happen. Type number two: those who watch things happen. And type number three: those who wonder what exactly happened. Well, our world is unfortunately made up of mostly the third type. They just wonder why in the world they're always in debt, they're always overweight, they're always in the poor job, they're always losing their job, they're always lonely, they're always miserable. They don't know why, they just kind of wonder what happened.

Then there's the second type of people, and some of them start to observe their surroundings more carefully. They become a little more self-aware and they begin to take more personal responsibility. As they do, they become sick of being in that third category. They watch the high achievers, the people of action, the people who make things happen. And some of that group begins to take full responsibility for their lives and join the first type, which is also known as the happiest and most fulfilled people—the people who make things happen.

Now I know that you all know that what I've said is absolutely true. You may not like it, but in your heart of hearts, you know it's true. The only barrier which separates you from achieving your dreams is to finally grow enough self-control or self-discipline to make it happen. To take the daily actions again and again, year after year, until you literally become a master of what you want to do, so good at it that people will pay you to do it. And that's happiness, because now you're doing what you want to do and you're getting paid for it instead of doing what somebody else wants you to do and getting paid less for it.

So I'm going to share with you now a few of my favorite quotes on self-control and self-discipline. I hope one or two of these will inspire you to decide you are going to grow your self-discipline and your self-control so that you can become more of what God knows that you can be by choosing to exercise your agency wisely.
Stephen Covey, a member of the church by the way, wrote this: "Only the disciplined are truly free. The undisciplined are slaves to moods, appetites, and passions."
Napoleon Hill, the author of Think and Grow Rich, wrote this: "Self-discipline begins with the mastery of your thoughts. If you don't control what you think, you cannot control what you do."
Epictetus, a Greek slave who rose to be a counselor to emperors in the Roman Empire, wrote this: "No man is free who is not master of himself."
Plato, the great philosopher, wrote this: "The first and best victory is to conquer self."
Horace, a writer of history, a wise man who lived about 2,000 years ago, wrote this: "Rule your mind or it will rule you."
Epictetus, again, that Greek slave who said so many wise things, said this: "Freedom is not procured by full enjoyment of what is desired, but by controlling that desire."
Aristotle, another great Greek philosopher, said this: "I count him braver who overcomes his desires than him who conquers his enemies. The hardest victory is the victory over self."

Vince Lombardi, a great American football coach, said this: "Leaders aren't born, they're made. And they are made just like anything else, through hard work. And that's the price we have to pay to achieve that goal or any goal."

And this one, also from Vince Lombardi, said: "Mental toughness is many things and rather difficult to explain. Its qualities are sacrifice and self-denial. Also, most importantly, it is combined with a perfectly disciplined will that refuses to give in. It's a state of mind—you could call it character in action."
William Feather said this: "If we don't discipline ourselves, the world will do it for us."
H. Jackson Brown said this: "Talent without discipline is like an octopus on roller skates. There's plenty of movement, but you never know if it's going to be forward, backward, or sideways."
John Foster said this: "A man without discipline of character can never be said to belong to himself. He belongs to whatever can make captive of him."

Henry Ward Beecher said this: "Hold yourself responsible for a higher standard than anybody else expects of you. Never excuse yourself, never pity yourself, be a hard master to yourself, and be lenient and kind to everybody else."
Paul Coffey said this: "Nobody's a natural. You work hard to get good and then you work harder to get better."
Angela Duckworth said this: "Talent plus effort becomes skill. Skill plus effort becomes success."

This final one, my favorite quote of all time on this topic of self-discipline, from Theodore Roosevelt, a president of the United States and one of my personal heroes: "The one quality which sets one man apart from another, the key which lifts one to every aspiration while others are caught up in the mire of mediocrity, is not talent, is not formal education, is not intellectual brightness—it is self-discipline. With self-discipline, all things are possible; without it, even the simplest goal can seem like the impossible dream."
Well, good night, sisters and elders. Rest well and choose to make the Sabbath a great day by exercising self-control. Love you.
